source: SEP (Priest, Berto, Weber) Paraconsistent Logic: history
finding: Paraconsistent logic starts with Jaskowski (1948, discussive logic in modal S5), da Costa (C-systems, dissertations from 1963), Priest (LP, 1979), Belnap (four-valued, 1977), relevant logics (Anderson and Belnap, Routley-Meyer) and adaptive logics (Batens).
numbers: Jaskowski discussive conjunction A and-d diamond B; discussive implication diamond A implies B. Six families named: discussive, C-systems/LFIs, LP, FDE/Belnap, relevant, adaptive.
limits: Secondary review. Dates of da Costa works given loosely.
agent_relevance: Gives the map of options for S6: each family is a different rule for how far a contradiction may spread.

source: SEP Paraconsistent Logic: LP truth tables and failed inferences
finding: LP has values t, f and b (both). Designated values are t and b. Negation swaps t and f and keeps b. Explosion fails: p=b and q=f makes p and not-p designated but q not. Modus ponens fails for the material conditional: p=b, q=f gives p-implies-q = b, so both premises designated, conclusion not. Disjunctive syllogism is not generally valid.
numbers: Counter-model for ECQ: v(p)=b, v(q)=f. Counter-model for MP: v(p)=b, v(q)=f, conditional=b.
quote: Disjunctive syllogism is not generally valid
limits: LP keeps excluded middle but loses the rules that carry a glut onward. Cost: weaker inference with the plain conditional.
agent_relevance: If the agent holds a conflicting pair, it must not chain from it by modus ponens or disjunctive syllogism without a check; code can enforce that.

source: SEP Paraconsistent Logic: LFIs and da Costa C-systems
finding: C1 is positive classical logic plus double negation elimination plus three axioms with a consistency operator: oA -> (A -> (not A -> B)); (oA and oB) -> o(A and B); (oA -> oB) -> o(A -> B). Hierarchy C_i for i>1 via A^1 = not(A and not A). Classical reasoning is recaptured by adding consistency assumptions: Gamma derives B classically iff o(Delta), Gamma derives B in the LFI.
numbers: Explosion restored only for formulas marked consistent (oA).
limits: C-omega is not an LFI because it lacks classical positive logic.
agent_relevance: Direct template: tag each claim as 'checked consistent' (a G3-style held-out pass) and allow classical chaining only for tagged claims.

source: SEP Paraconsistent Logic: adaptive logics
finding: An adaptive logic has a lower limit logic, a set of abnormalities (often A and not A) and a strategy. The upper limit logic adds rules like disjunctive syllogism. Worked example with premises {p, not p or r, not r or s, not s, s or t}: a derivation of t by disjunctive syllogism lapses once s and not s is derived.
numbers: Derived lines are retracted when an abnormality involving them appears.
limits: The excerpt did not describe dynamic-proof marking in detail.
agent_relevance: Closest formal match to an agent that reasons classically by default and withdraws only the conclusions touched by a found conflict.

source: SEP Paraconsistent Logic: chunk and permeate
finding: Chunk and permeate keeps consistent chunks Sigma_i and a permeability relation rho. Stages: Sigma_i^0 = closure of Sigma_i; Sigma_i^(n+1) = closure of (Sigma_i^n plus the part of Sigma_j^n allowed by rho(j,i)). Consequences are read in a designated chunk i0. Motivated by Leibniz infinitesimals and Bohr's atom.
limits: Needs a hand-built permeability relation.
agent_relevance: Matches keeping two incompatible candidate hypotheses in separate contexts and letting only chosen facts cross between them.

source: SEP (Priest, Berto, Weber) Dialetheism: arguments and Priest's Rationality Principle
finding: Priest's main argument is the liar, plus other self-reference paradoxes under a principle of uniform solution. Curry's paradox forces dropping contraction. Consistency is one epistemic virtue among adequacy to data, simplicity and explanatory power. Priest's Rationality Principle: with good evidence for A, accept A. Rejection is a separate act from accepting a negation.
limits: The entry does not cover empirical studies or the quasi-validity reply to disjunctive syllogism.
agent_relevance: Design point: 'reject' and 'accept not-A' are different states; the agent can hold a claim as neither accepted nor rejected.

source: Jakl (2025) Four imprints of Belnap's useful four-valued logic in computer science
finding: Belnap's four values are True, False, None (no information) and Both (inconsistent). Key idea: two orders on the lattice, the logical order and the information (knowledge) order, inspired by domain theory. Ginsberg bilattices generalise it; Fitting showed the construction works for any lattice; Rivieccio showed every bilattice has a twist-product form. Links to linear logic, d-frames, Blame Calculus, LVars.
quote: Belnap was the first to identify the two orders and stress the use of four values for computer reasoning
limits: Survey of theory; no empirical test.
agent_relevance: Both and None are separate states. An agent with only true/false confuses 'two sources disagree' with 'no source says anything'.

source: Belnap (1977) A useful four-valued logic, in Modern Uses of Multiple-Valued Logic
finding: A computer fed by several sources may hold: told true only, told false only, told both, told neither. Motivation was database inconsistency and avoiding run-away inferences from (A and not A) to B. Now called Belnap-Dunn logic or FDE.
limits: Not opened. Known only from search snippets and the Jakl survey; one snippet confused the title with Shramko and Wansing (2005) sixteen-valued logics.
agent_relevance: Original source for the 'combine reports from several sources' framing of conflict.

source: Priest (1979) The Logic of Paradox, Journal of Philosophical Logic 8:219-241
finding: Introduces LP: three values with an extra 'paradoxical' value for both true and false; designated values true and paradoxical. Made the logic well known and tied it to dialetheism.
limits: Not opened (paywalled). Framing from search snippet.
agent_relevance: Founding paper; the design uses its ideas through secondary sources only.

source: Alxatib and Pelletier (2011) The Psychology of Vagueness: Borderline Cases and Contradictions, Mind and Language 26(3):287-326
finding: Core human test of gluts versus gaps. 76 SFU undergraduates did a 20-item true/false/can't-tell survey on a picture of men of different heights. For the 5 ft 11 (borderline) man, 34 of 76 (44.7%) judged 'tall and not tall' TRUE, 31 (40.8%) FALSE, 11 (14.5%) can't tell. So more than half were not classicalists.
numbers: N=76; 63.2% native English speakers. 'x is neither tall nor not tall' true for 53.9% at the midpoint, false 42.1%. 'Both' true peaked at 44.7%, false minimum 40.8%.
limits: One student sample, one adjective (tall). Authors say the data are no knock-down case for any theory; a pragmatic reading of 'not tall' may drive answers.
agent_relevance: People accept some contradictions at borderline cases. Humans are partly paraconsistent, but the effect is tied to vagueness, not to contradictions in general.

source: Alxatib and Pelletier (2011): gap and glut overlap
finding: Among those who judged 'neither tall nor not tall' true for the 5 ft 11 man, 53.7% also judged 'tall and not tall' true, 31.7% false and 14.6% can't tell. Same answer to 'tall' and 'not tall': both true 3.9%, both false 21.0%, both can't-tell 5.3%.
numbers: Gap-style and glut-style answers come from the same people in over half of cases.
limits: Hard to separate gap from glut readings; no between-subject control.
agent_relevance: Gap (neither) and glut (both) coexist; the agent's state space should allow both, as Belnap's four values do.

source: Alxatib and Pelletier (2011): asymmetry between denying and asserting
finding: At 5 ft 11, 46.1% said 'tall' is true but 67.1% said 'not tall' is false; 25.0% said 'not tall' is true but 44.7% said 'tall' is false. Subjects deny a statement more readily than they assent to its negation. 'Can't tell' stayed small: 9.2% for 'tall', 7.9% for 'not tall'.
numbers: 'Tall' true: 1.3% at 5 ft 4, median 46.1% at 5 ft 11, 98.7% at 6 ft 6.
limits: Authors note an error-avoidance reading.
agent_relevance: Rejecting is easier than asserting the negation: supports keeping 'rejected' separate from 'believed false'.

source: Follow-ups on borderline contradictions: Ripley (2011), Egre and colleagues, Alxatib, Pagin and Sauerland (2013)
finding: Several studies, including Ripley (2011), report that contradiction-like sentences about borderline cases are accepted to a significant extent. Egre and colleagues tested gaps versus gluts with relative gradable adjectives. Alxatib, Pagin and Sauerland (2013) asked if acceptance is pragmatic or semantic. A quantum-probability paper fitted a classical probability model to the 2011 data and found no fully satisfactory fit.
limits: Not opened: search snippets only. Numbers not retrieved.
agent_relevance: Acceptance of borderline contradictions replicates, but the cause (pragmatic or semantic) stays disputed.

source: Allen, Chhikara, Ferguson, Ilievski, Groth (2025) Sound and Complete Neurosymbolic Reasoning with LLM-Grounded Interpretations (NeSy 2025, PMLR 284)
finding: An LLM judge gives each atomic claim a pair: can it verify it, can it refute it. This yields a Belnap-style value (true only, false only, both = glut, neither = gap) inside a paraconsistent logic (Angell's analytic containment, ACrQ). Bilateral evaluation raised macro-F1 over a true/false baseline by about 6 points on both benchmarks, at the price of coverage.
numbers: Table 1 (N=400 per dataset, 200 correct + 200 wrong): GPQA flagship F1 0.699 vs 0.633 unilateral (coverage 0.589 vs 1.0); GPQA distilled 0.608 vs 0.559 (0.504); SimpleQA flagship 0.736 vs 0.657 (0.584); SimpleQA distilled 0.624 vs 0.570 (0.499). Bootstrap SEs about 0.01; paired t-tests.
quote: Repeated sampling (N=3) with majority vote was used in both the verification and refutation processes.
limits: Gain is on non-abstained items only; coverage falls about 0.46. Accuracy, precision, recall not reported. Negatives partly synthetic (GPT-4o Mini). Not a full Belnap computer.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of paraconsistent handling: a conflict flag lets the agent abstain or escalate instead of guessing. Trade is higher precision for fewer answers.

source: Allen et al. (2025): per-model results
finding: Bilateral macro-F1 varies widely by model and prompt. Best GPQA: Llama 4 Maverick 0.774 (direct). Best SimpleQA: GPT-4o few-shot CoT 0.833. Worst: GPT-4o Mini zero-shot GPQA 0.400. Prompt-style effects are large and inconsistent across models.
limits: Temperature 0.1, 3 samples; mid-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one prompt style; the value of a conflict flag depends on the judge model.

source: Allen et al. (2025): how often LLM judges return gluts and gaps (journal version, Tables 3 and 14)
finding: LLM judges often return a glut (verify and refute both). GPT models average 59.0% gluts with near-zero gaps (under 0.1%) on SimpleQA topics. Claude models: glut 19.6%, gap 30.4%. Llama: glut 52.9%, verified-only 29.8%. Video games glut 63.6%, sports 47.3%, history lowest 35.7%.
numbers: Table 3 (GPQA flagship): (t,t) 0.301, (t,f) 0.211, (f,t) 0.378, (f,f) 0.110. Distilled: 0.299/0.192/0.312/0.197. Table 14: ten SimpleQA topics, zero-shot.
limits: Rates depend on prompt wording; authors say gaps partly come from poor verbalization while gluts reflect contradictory parametric knowledge.
agent_relevance: Model families differ in epistemic style: GPT-like judges say 'both', Claude-like say 'neither'. A glut-based impasse detector needs per-model calibration.

source: Allen et al. (2025): medication-safety knowledge base demonstration
finding: Proof-of-concept tableau reasoner with GPT-4o as judge: 228 asserted statements (28 rules, 200 ground facts, 16 drug classes) plus 712 forward-chained = 940. It found 92 gluts and 2 gaps while the theory stayed satisfiable, so contradictions were localised and nothing exploded. Gluts: 25 opioids 'nonaddictive', 30 benzodiazepines, 11 antipsychotics, 11 beta-blockers safe in asthma, 7 fluoroquinolones in children.
numbers: SAT with 92 gluts; Table 4 (940 statements).
quote: Despite 92 contradictions, the theory remained satisfiable.
limits: Authors call it deliberately artificial: rules were seeded with errors. No precision/recall of glut detection; one judge model.
agent_relevance: Closest existing demo of S6: keep working over a set with known conflicts, report which conclusions are contested, do not collapse.

source: Allen et al. (2025): theorems and stated limits
finding: Soundness (Thm 10) and completeness (Thm 11) of tableau system ACrQ with respect to LLM-grounded interpretations, building on Ferguson (2021). The logic is paraconsistent and paracomplete, uses weak-Kleene values paired into generalised truth values, and is related to FDE. Limits: about 2k API calls per atom for k samples; worst case exponential in number of atoms; only the atomic valuation was tested.
numbers: Cost per item: bilateral 30-37 s and 3,964-4,782 tokens vs unilateral 11-13 s and 2,100-2,500 tokens.
limits: QA pairs used as proxy for atoms; no real KB benchmark.
agent_relevance: Doubling judge calls is the price of a conflict signal; use only where a signal is needed (G1).

source: Hou et al. (2024) WikiContradict: benchmark for LLMs on real-world knowledge conflicts from Wikipedia
finding: 253 human-annotated instances from Wikipedia contradiction tags (161 explicit, 92 implicit). Given two conflicting passages with no cue, models almost never answer in a way that reflects both: 2.1% to 10.4% correct. With a cue to consider conflicts it rises, best Llama-3-70b 43.8%, GPT-4 only 10.4%.
numbers: No cue: Mistral-7b 2.1, Mixtral 4.2, Llama-2-70b 4.2, Llama-3-70b 10.4, GPT-4 6.3. Cue: 20.8, 14.6, 22.9, 43.8, 10.4. Single-passage questions 82.9-97.6% correct. Llama-3-70b explicit conflicts 13.3% -> 60.0% with cue, implicit 5.9% -> 17.6%.
limits: Human eval on 48 instances / 1,200 responses; Cohen kappa 0.58 to 0.88; text and abstract disagree on judgement counts; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Default LLM behaviour with contradictory evidence is to silently pick one side. A paraconsistent state must be forced by the scaffold.

source: Hou et al. (2024) WikiContradict: detection and automatic judging
finding: Models can detect contradictions when asked: GPT-4 about 88%, Llama-3-70b about 77%. But with conflict-free context and a request to list contradictions, GPT-4 confirmed conflict-free only 44% and Llama-3-70b 48%. Judge accuracy on 240 human-labelled responses: GPT-4 86.7%, Llama-3-70b 85.4%, GPT-4o 83.3%, Mixtral 26.2%.
numbers: Macro-F: GPT-4 76.1, Llama-3-70b 74.4, GPT-4o 71.3. Judge over-rates Mistral-7b (39.6% vs 20.8% human).
limits: Appendix variants used one annotator per response.
agent_relevance: Models can flag conflicts but also invent false ones about half the time; a conflict flag needs a code check.

source: Li et al. (2025) Don't Take the Premise for Granted: Premise Critique Bench (PCBench)
finding: 1,200 base math problems x 3 variants = 3,600; four error types (contradictory premise, contradictory inference, flawed solution, irrelevant query); 15 LLMs (7 non-reasoning, 8 reasoning). Without a prompt to check, models rarely flag the flaw; with an explicit instruction they do much more.
numbers: Proactive rate from 4.0% (o4-mini) to 40.5% (DeepSeek-V3); assisted from 53.5% (Llama-4-Maverick) to 77.9% (Gemini-2.0-flash-thinking). GPT-4o 11.0% proactive; GPT-4.1 73.2% assisted. Output length ratio up to 3.90 (o3-mini).
quote: Most models show limited ability to autonomously critique flawed premises
limits: Easy subset numbers; no consistent correlation between reasoning strength and premise critique.
agent_relevance: With contradictory inputs models continue silently; the scaffold must make the conflict visible.

source: PCBench: reasoning models notice but do not report
finding: In a DeepSeek-R1 case the chain of thought repeatedly flagged the conflict ('Wait, let me check again') but the final answer chose one condition and never reported it. Similar gaps for o3-mini-medium and o4-mini.
numbers: Case-level observations, not rates.
limits: Anecdotal examples.
agent_relevance: Inconsistency is detected internally and then collapsed at output: the 'drop one side' failure the paraconsistent state should prevent.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Self-Contradictory Reasoning Evaluation and Detection (Self-Contra)
finding: Self-contradictory reasoning rates (SCR) on WinoBias, WinoGrande, WinoGender (three datasets). GPT-3.5 zero-shot answer-first SCR 0.28/0.60/0.30; few-shot 0.32/0.26/0.18; Mistral 7B zero-shot 0.48/0.42/0.24; Claude 3 zero-shot 0.10/0.12/0.06, few-shot 0.10/0.02/0.04. Accuracy and SCR correlate at r=-0.634 (p=0.006) overall, but not for GPT-3.5 (p=0.676) or Mistral (p=0.083).
numbers: Three types: correct reasoning with wrong answer, wrong reasoning with right answer, reasoning that contradicts itself. Temperature 0. Column order in the table follows the paper's dataset order.
limits: Pronoun-resolution tasks only; small samples.
agent_relevance: Accuracy does not rule out internal contradiction; a reasoning-versus-answer check is a separate signal.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Self-Contra: detection by GPT-4
finding: GPT-4 detects self-contradictory reasoning at only 52.2% F1 versus 66.7% for humans. Detection via finer-grained categories beats binary prompting by 10 to 15 F1 points. GPT-3.5 reasoning on WB Anti: binary F1 0.253, finer-grained 0.522; Mistral WB Anti: binary 0.595, finer-grained 0.543.
numbers: Binary vs finer-grained F1 per dataset in Table 6.
limits: Mixed result: finer-grained better for GPT-3.5, not for Mistral WB Anti.
agent_relevance: Models are poor judges of their own contradictions (G2): put detection in code or in decomposed checks.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) MOSAIC: long-term memory for LLM agents with save-time conflict detection
finding: Agent memory checks each new fact against graph neighbours at save time and updates or deletes contradicting entries. Detected 66% of injected factual conflicts versus 14% for the best baseline (4.7x). LoCoMo accuracy 89.35% (+27.21 points).
numbers: HaluMem-Medium extraction F1 86.77%, Long 85.84%; QA correctness 73.10% and 70.75%; latency 0.58 s per question.
limits: Resolution is update-or-delete, which is the classical choice, not paraconsistent retention. Abstract only; detection method not described.
agent_relevance: Contradiction handling in agent memory pays off, but it deletes, so the lost side is gone.

source: Zheng et al. (2025, rev. 2026) KCR: Disentangling Reasoning Logic to Resolve Explicit Knowledge Conflicts
finding: Splits conflicting contexts into separate reasoning traces with a hybrid text and graph form and trains with RL with verifiable rewards. A 7B model with KCR beats GPT-4o and GPT-5.1 on adjudication of conflicting retrieved contexts.
numbers: No metrics in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Trained method, not a scaffold; it picks the consistent trace, so it adjudicates rather than holds both.
agent_relevance: Separating conflicting contexts into traces is chunk-and-permeate in practice.

source: Ongaratto and van Ditmarsch (2026) The Dynamic Turn in Paraconsistency
finding: Dynamic epistemic paraconsistent logics: AMLFI1 (action models over LFI1), a paraconsistent public announcement logic PALFI1, and UMLFI1 with factual change. Soundness and completeness proved. Meant to formalise how provisional contradictions arise and are resolved.
limits: Pure logic; no implementation or test.
agent_relevance: A formal frame for 'hold the conflict now, resolve when an announcement or check arrives', matching S6 exit rules.

source: arXiv scan: query 'paraconsistent' (182 hits) and related queries
finding: Of 182 hits almost all are formal logic. Only two of the 25 newest touch ML: ParaQNN (2601.12635, neural net with a 'dialetheist logic layer' for open quantum systems, no numbers in abstract) and an LLM output-format paper that matched by keyword only. Others: Eliano (2607.09729) AGM-like paraconsistent abductive expansion; Coniglio and Ongaratto (2604.18766) a taxonomy for controlling inconsistency. Allen et al. 2025 is the only LLM study found with a paraconsistent logic at its core.
numbers: Queries 'Belnap four-valued LLM' and 'contradictory premises LLM explosion' returned zero hits.
limits: Title/abstract search only; page truncated at about 46 results. Titles other than those opened are from the listing.
agent_relevance: The empirical LLM literature on paraconsistent reasoning is thin: one main study. Most evidence for S6 will have to be our own tests.

source: Gao, Fodor, Kifer (2016) Paraconsistency and Word Puzzles
finding: Uses annotated predicate calculus with a new semantics to handle inconsistent information in word puzzles, implemented in Clingo.
limits: Not opened: abstract gist from an arXiv search listing.
agent_relevance: Earlier example of paraconsistent logic in a puzzle solver; relevant to our word puzzles.

source: CounterLogic: logical reasoning in counterfactual worlds (arXiv 2505.22318, via search snippet)
finding: Across 11 LLMs and six datasets, accuracy falls on average by 27% when valid arguments have premises that conflict with world knowledge; authors attribute it to knowledge conflicts, not weak logic.
limits: Not opened: search snippet only; authors not checked.
agent_relevance: Conflict between premises and priors is a second kind of contradiction the agent meets and it lowers accuracy.
